Functions & Modularity

docs.title: Core Data Structures
docs.text:
90 min Python Needs: Functions & Modularity

Real programs work with collections: a list of users, a grid of values, a set of tags, a table of prices. Python has four built-in collections, and each is good at one thing. This tutorial covers all four, how to use them without crashing on unexpected input, and the one behaviour that surprises everyone: two names for the same list.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Choosing the right collection makes code shorter, faster and easier to read. Checking whether a word is in a set of ten thousand words is instant; in a list, Python checks them one by one.

The other half of this page is about edge cases: empty lists, missing keys, repeated values, indices that do not exist. Your code will meet all of them, because real data is messy and the Checker tests with exactly these inputs on purpose.

docs.title: The four collections
docs.text: Example Ordered Changeable Duplicates Use it for list [3, 1, 3] yes yes yes A sequence you add to, change and loop over tuple (3, 4) yes no yes A fixed group of values, such as a point or several return values set {1, 3} no yes no Unique items, membership tests, comparing groups dict {"a": 1} yes yes keys: no Looking values up by a key

docs.title: Step 1: Lists
docs.text:
A list is an ordered, changeable sequence. Indexing and slicing work exactly as they do on strings.

langs = ["python", "c", "javascript"]
langs[0]               # 'python'
langs[-1]              # 'javascript'
len(langs)             # 3

langs.append("sql")    # add to the end
langs.insert(1, "bash")
langs.pop()            # remove and return the last item: 'sql'
langs.remove("c")      # remove the first "c"
"go" in langs          # False

Unlike strings, lists are mutable: append, insert, pop and remove change the list itself and return nothing useful (except pop). Compare two ways to sort:

nums = [3, 1, 2]
s = sorted(nums)       # a NEW sorted list; nums is unchanged
nums.sort()            # sorts nums itself; returns None

new_list = old_list.sort() is a common bug: new_list is None.

docs.title: Loop with or without the index
docs.text:
for lang in langs:                 # when you only need the items
    print(lang)

for i in range(len(langs)):        # when you need the position too
    print(i, langs[i])

docs.title: Step 2: Two names, one list
docs.text:
This is the behaviour behind most list bugs.

Assignment shares a list; copy makes a new one After b equals a, both names point to the same list object, so appending through b also changes what a shows. After c equals a dot copy, c points to a separate new list, so changing c leaves a alone. b = a two names, one list a b [1, 2, 3, 4] b.append(4) → a is [1, 2, 3, 4] too c = a.copy() two names, two lists a c [1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] c.append(5) → a is unchanged

A variable does not hold a list. It points to one. b = a does not copy anything; it gives the same list a second name.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3, 4]  a changed too: it is the same list

c = a.copy()    # a.copy(), a[:] and list(a) all make a new list
c.append(5)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3, 4]  unchanged
print(c)        # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

The same thing happens when you pass a list to a function. The parameter is another name for the caller's list, so a function that changes it changes the caller's data:

def add_bonus(scores):           # changes the list it was given
    for i in range(len(scores)):
        scores[i] += 5


def with_bonus(scores):          # builds and returns a new list
    return [s + 5 for s in scores]


marks = [70, 85]
new = with_bonus(marks)          # marks is still [70, 85]; new is [75, 90]
add_bonus(marks)                 # marks is now [75, 90]

Both are valid. What matters is that the function's name and docstring make clear which one it does. When a task says without modifying the original, build and return a new collection.

docs.title: Build a new list with a comprehension
docs.text:
The with_bonus function used a list comprehension: a short way to build a new list from an existing one.

[n * 2 for n in [1, 2, 3]]                 # [2, 4, 6]
[n for n in [4, 7, 10, 13] if n % 2 == 0]  # [4, 10]  only the even ones

Read it as "this expression, for each item, if this condition". It never changes the original list.

docs.title: Step 3: Access elements safely
docs.text:
items[i] raises an IndexError when i is out of range. When a function should cope with bad input instead of crashing, check first:

def item_at(items, index):
    """Return the item at index, or None if there is none."""
    if index < 0 or index >= len(items):
        return None
    return items[index]


item_at(["a", "b"], 1)     # 'b'
item_at(["a", "b"], 5)     # None
item_at([], 0)             # None: the empty list is handled too

Note the decision to reject negative indices. Python would accept items[-1], but if the task defines index as a position counted from 0, a negative number is invalid input. Read what the task means by valid, then check exactly that.

The same idea, without changing the original:

def replaced(items, index, value):
    """Return a copy of items with one element replaced."""
    copy = items[:]
    if 0 <= index < len(items):
        copy[index] = value
    return copy

docs.title: Step 4: Matrices
docs.text:
A matrix is a list of lists: each inner list is a row.

A matrix as a list of rows grid has two rows and three columns. grid at 0 is the row 1, 2, 3; grid at 1 is the row 4, 5, 6. grid at 1, 2 picks row 1, then column 2 inside it, which is 6. The outer loop goes over rows and the inner loop over the numbers in each row. col 0col 1col 2 grid[0] grid[1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 grid[1][2] → 6 row 1 first, then column 2 each row is a list len(grid) = 2, len(grid[0]) = 3 outer loop: rows · inner loop: numbers in the row 
grid = [[1, 2, 3],
        [4, 5, 6]]

grid[1][2]     # 6: row 1, then column 2
len(grid)      # 2 rows
len(grid[0])   # 3 columns

To print it, loop over rows, and over the numbers in each row. The cleanest way to put exactly one space between numbers, and none at the end, is join, which glues strings together with a separator:

for row in grid:
    print(" ".join(str(n) for n in row))

1 2 3
4 5 6

join only accepts strings, so each number is converted with str first, or with an f-string such as f"{n:2}" to align columns. A comprehension inside a comprehension builds a new matrix and leaves the original alone:

times_ten = [[n * 10 for n in row] for row in grid]
# [[10, 20, 30], [40, 50, 60]]; grid is unchanged

Edge case: an empty matrix, [[]], has one row with no numbers. The loop above prints one empty line, which is usually exactly what the task expects.

docs.title: Step 5: Tuples
docs.text:
A tuple is like a list that cannot be changed. Use one for a fixed group of values that belong together.

point = (3, 4)
x, y = point          # unpacking: x is 3, y is 4
point[0] = 1          # TypeError: tuples cannot be changed
x, y = y, x           # swap two variables in one line

Tuples are the clean way to return several values from a function. return a, b returns a tuple, and the caller unpacks it:

def min_max(numbers):
    """Return the smallest and largest number, or (None, None) if empty."""
    if not numbers:
        return None, None
    return min(numbers), max(numbers)


low, high = min_max([4, 9, 1])    # low is 1, high is 9
min_max([])                       # (None, None)

Notice the empty case returns the same shape: two values. The caller can always write low, high = min_max(...) without checking first. Returning a single None there would crash the unpacking.

docs.title: Step 6: Sets
docs.text:
A set holds unique values, in no particular order. Its strength is comparing groups.

Intersection and symmetric difference of two sets Alice knows python, git and sql. Bob knows git, javascript and python. The intersection, alice and bob, is the overlap: git and python. The symmetric difference, alice caret bob, is everything in exactly one of the two sets: sql and javascript. alice bob sql git python javascript alice & bob alice bob sql git python javascript alice ^ bob 
alice = {"python", "git", "sql"}
bob = {"git", "javascript", "python"}

alice & bob     # intersection:         {'git', 'python'}   in both
alice | bob     # union:                all four            in either
alice - bob     # difference:           {'sql'}             only in alice
alice ^ bob     # symmetric difference: {'javascript', 'sql'}  in exactly one

Sets also remove duplicates: set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]) is {1, 2, 3}, and len(set(items)) counts the distinct values in a list.

Sets have no order

Printing a set can show its items in any order, and the order may change between runs. When output must be exact, sort it first: sorted(alice & bob) always gives ['git', 'python'].

docs.title: Step 7: Dictionaries
docs.text:
A dictionary maps keys to values. You look a value up by its key, not by a position.

stock = {"apples": 5, "pears": 2}

stock["apples"]          # 5
stock["kiwis"]           # KeyError: 'kiwis'
stock.get("kiwis")       # None: no error
stock.get("kiwis", 0)    # 0: a default of your choice
"pears" in stock         # True: `in` checks keys

stock["kiwis"] = 7       # add a new key
stock["apples"] += 1     # update an existing one
del stock["pears"]       # remove a key (KeyError if it is missing)

Loop over keys, or over keys and values together. For exact output, sort the keys:

for name in sorted(stock):
    print(f"{name}: {stock[name]}")

for name, qty in stock.items():
    ...

apples: 6
kiwis: 7

A dictionary is the natural way to count repeated values. Use get with a default of 0, so the first time a word appears is not a special case:

words = ["git", "python", "git", "sql", "git"]
counts = {}
for word in words:
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
# {'git': 3, 'python': 1, 'sql': 1}

docs.title: Step 8: Think about edge cases first
docs.text:
Before you write a function, list the awkward inputs and decide what it should do with each. Most failed checks are one of these.

Input Question to ask Usual answer Empty list [] What is the max of nothing? Return None, or the documented default Index out of range, or negative Crash, or return something? Check bounds; follow the task Missing key d[key] or d.get(key)? get with a default when missing is normal Repeated values Count them, or once each? dict to count, set to deduplicate None passed instead of a list Is that valid input? Check if items is None if the task allows it Original must not change Am I mutating it? Build and return a new collection

Then test the function with each of them, not only with the friendly example from the task.

AI in the loop

Assistants are good at finding edge cases you missed. Write your function first, then ask: "List inputs that could break this function or make it return something unexpected. Don't fix the code." Test each one yourself. Asking for the cases rather than the fix keeps the reasoning on your side.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
My original list changed and I did not touch it

Somewhere you have two names for one list: an assignment such as b = a, or a function that modifies its parameter. Copy with a[:] or a.copy(), or build a new list.

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...

You stored the result of a method that changes a list in place, such as nums = nums.sort(). Use nums.sort() on its own line, or nums = sorted(nums).

KeyError with a dictionary

The key is not there. Check with key in d, or read it with d.get(key, default).

My set output is in a different order from the expected output

Sets have no order. Sort before printing.

TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, int found

join needs strings. Convert each item: " ".join(str(n) for n in row).

docs.title: Environment & First Programs
docs.text:
45 min Python Needs: WSL, VS Code

Before you write real programs, you need to know the two ways Python runs code, how to turn a file into a program you can run like any other command, and how to keep each project's packages separate. This tutorial covers all three.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Most beginner confusion in Python is not about the language. It is about the environment: code that prints in one place and not another, a package that is installed but "not found", a script that works on your laptop and fails on the Checker. Each of those has a simple cause, and you will meet all of them in this tutorial on purpose.

docs.title: Two ways to run Python
docs.text:
Interactive mode compared with a script In interactive mode you type one line at a time after the three-arrow prompt, and Python shows the value of every expression automatically: typing 2 plus 3 shows 5. In a script, Python runs the whole file from top to bottom and shows nothing unless you call print: the line 2 plus 3 produces no output, and print of 2 plus 3 prints 5. INTERACTIVE MODE python3 >>> 2 + 3 5 >>> x = 10 >>> x * 2 20 value shown for you statement: no output SCRIPT ./calc.py 2 + 3 print(2 + 3) $ ./calc.py 5 computed, then thrown away printed

Interactive mode is for trying things. You type one line, Python runs it and shows you the result straight away. A script is a file Python runs from top to bottom. It is what you submit for projects, and it shows only what you explicitly print.

docs.title: Step 1: Use the interpreter
docs.text:
Open the Ubuntu terminal and start the interpreter:

python3

Python 3.12.3 (main, ...) [GCC 13.2.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>

The >>> is Python's prompt, the same idea as the shell's $. Leave with exit() or Ctrl+D.

docs.title: Expressions and statements
docs.text:
Python code is made of two kinds of thing.

  • An expression produces a value: 2 + 3, "hi".upper(), len("abc"), x * 2.
  • A statement does something: x = 10 stores a value, import math loads a module, if and for control what runs.

In interactive mode, when you type an expression on its own, Python shows its value. When you type a statement, it shows nothing, because there is no value to show. Predict each line, then try it:

You type Python shows Why 7 * 6 42 Expression: value shown answer = 7 * 6 nothing Assignment is a statement answer 42 Expression: value shown "python".upper() 'PYTHON' Expression, shown as Python writes it, with quotes print("python".upper()) PYTHON print writes the text itself, no quotes import math nothing Statement math.sqrt(16) 4.0 Expression

Look closely at the fourth and fifth rows. The interpreter shows a value the way you would type it in code ('PYTHON', with quotes). print shows it the way a person would read it (PYTHON). In a script only the second kind of output exists.

Ask Python, not Google

The interpreter has its own manual. help(str) describes every string method, help(print) describes print, and dir("text") lists everything you can call on a string. Press Q to leave a help page.

docs.title: Step 2: Write a portable, executable script
docs.text:
Make a folder for this module and a first script:

mkdir -p ~/holberton/python-basics
cd ~/holberton/python-basics
code calc.py
calc.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
2 + 3
print(2 + 3)

Make it executable and run it:

chmod u+x calc.py
./calc.py

You see 5 once. The bare 2 + 3 was calculated and thrown away, because a script never shows values on its own.

docs.title: Why #!/usr/bin/env python3
docs.text:
The first line is the shebang you met in Shell Basics. You could write #!/usr/bin/python3, but that only works on machines where Python lives at exactly that path. /usr/bin/env python3 asks the system to find python3 wherever it is installed, including inside the virtual environment you build in Step 4. That is what makes the script portable.

An executable script needs three things: the shebang on the first line, execute permission from chmod u+x, and Unix line endings (see When something goes wrong).

docs.title: Step 3: Global installs and isolated environments
docs.text:
pip installs Python packages. The question is where.

Global installation compared with virtual environments With a global installation, every project shares one set of packages in the system Python, so project A needing version 1 of a library and project B needing version 2 conflict. With virtual environments, each project has its own dot venv folder with its own packages, so the two versions live side by side and the system Python stays clean. GLOBAL: ONE SHARED SET System Python requests 1.x or 2.x? project A needs 1.x project B needs 2.x conflict: only one version fits ISOLATED: ONE VENV PER PROJECT System Python stays clean project A .venv requests 1.x project B .venv requests 2.x each project gets exactly what it needs

A global installation puts a package into the Python that the whole system shares. Every project sees it, which sounds convenient until two projects need different versions of the same package, or an install breaks a tool Ubuntu itself relies on.

A virtual environment, or venv, is a folder inside your project with its own copy of pip and its own packages. Activate it and Python uses that folder; deactivate it and you are back to the system. Nothing leaks between projects.

Recent Ubuntu versions enforce this. Try a global install:

pip install pycodestyle

error: externally-managed-environment
× This environment is externally managed

That error is Ubuntu protecting its own Python. It is pointing you at the right answer: a virtual environment.

docs.title: Step 4: Isolate a project with venv
docs.text:
Create a venv in your project folder and activate it:

cd ~/holberton/python-basics
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

Your prompt now starts with (.venv). Check which Python you are using:

which python3

/home/you/holberton/python-basics/.venv/bin/python3

That path is inside your project. Now install a development tool: pycodestyle, which checks your code against Python's official style guide. You use it in every project from the next tutorial on.

pip install pycodestyle
pycodestyle --version
pycodestyle calc.py

No error this time. Record what the project needs, so anyone can rebuild the same environment:

pip freeze > requirements.txt
cat requirements.txt

Now see the isolation for yourself:

deactivate
pycodestyle --version      # command not found: it only exists in the venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pycodestyle --version      # back again

The tool exists inside the environment and nowhere else. That is the whole idea.

A few habits to keep:

  • One venv per project, named .venv, inside the project folder.
  • Never commit it. Add .venv/ to your .gitignore. Commit requirements.txt instead; anyone can rebuild the venv with pip install -r requirements.txt.
  • Activate it every time you open a new terminal for the project. If (.venv) is missing from the prompt, you are using the system Python.

Point VS Code at the venv

Press Ctrl+Shift+P, run Python: Select Interpreter and pick the one in ./.venv. VS Code then activates it in every new terminal and uses its packages for error checking.

AI in the loop

When you hit the externally-managed-environment error, an assistant may suggest --break-system-packages. Ask it what that flag breaks before you consider it. The honest answer is in the name: use a venv instead. This is a good habit in general: when a fix contains the words force or break, find out why.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
/usr/bin/env: 'python3\r': No such file or directory

The file has Windows line endings (CRLF). Linux reads the invisible \r as part of the program name. In VS Code, click CRLF in the status bar and change it to LF, then save. To stop it happening again, add "files.eol": "\n" to your VS Code settings.

Permission denied when running ./script.py

It is not executable yet. Run chmod u+x script.py.

The virtual environment was not created successfully because ensurepip is not available

Ubuntu's venv support is a separate package. Run sudo apt install -y python3-venv, then create the venv again.

python: command not found

Ubuntu calls it python3. Use python3, or inside an active venv, python also works.

I installed a package but Python says ModuleNotFoundError

You installed it in one environment and ran Python from another. Check the prompt shows (.venv) and that which python3 points inside your project, then install again.

docs.title: Exception Handling
docs.text:
60 min Python Needs: Core Data Structures

Programs fail. A user types letters where you expected a number, a list is empty, a key is missing. An exception is how Python reports a failure while the program is running. This tutorial shows you how to read one, catch the ones you expect, raise your own, and write functions that fail in a way their callers can rely on.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
There are two bad ways to deal with errors: ignore them, so the program crashes on the first odd input, or swallow all of them, so it carries on with wrong data and nobody knows why. Good code sits between the two. It handles the failures it expects, in a precise and visible way, and lets real bugs surface.

In the previous tutorial you prevented errors by checking first. This one adds the other tool: try it, and handle the failure. You need both.

docs.title: Step 1: Read a traceback
docs.text:
When an exception is not handled, Python stops and prints a traceback. Most people read it from the top. Read it from the bottom.

avg.py
def average(numbers):
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)


print(average([4, 8]))
print(average([]))

6.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/you/holberton/python-basics/avg.py", line 6, in <module>
    print(average([]))
          ~~~~~~~^^^^
  File "/home/you/holberton/python-basics/avg.py", line 2, in average
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
  1. The last line says what went wrong: the exception type, ZeroDivisionError, and a message.
  2. The frame above it says where: line 2, inside average. The ^ marks point at the exact operation.
  3. The frames above that say how you got there: line 6 called average with an empty list.

The fix is rarely on the last line of code shown. Here the division is fine; the question is what average should do with an empty list.

docs.title: Step 2: Know the common exceptions
docs.text:
Each exception type names a different kind of mistake. Recognising them on sight tells you where to look.

Exception Raised when Example TypeError A value is the wrong type for the operation "3" + 4 ValueError The type is right but the value is not int("forty") IndexError A list index is out of range [1, 2][5] KeyError A dictionary key is missing {"a": 1}["b"] ZeroDivisionError Dividing by zero 10 / 0 NameError A name is not defined, often a typo prnt("hi") AttributeError The object has no such method or attribute "text".push("x") FileNotFoundError A file to open does not exist open("missing.txt")

docs.title: Step 3: Catch a specific exception
docs.text:
Put the code that might fail in a try block, and say what to do if it fails in an except block naming the exception:

def ratio(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("b must not be zero")
    except TypeError:
        print("a and b must be numbers")
    return None


ratio(6, 3)       # 2.0
ratio(6, 0)       # prints "b must not be zero", returns None
ratio("6", 3)     # prints "a and b must be numbers", returns None

Python runs the try block. If an exception is raised, it jumps straight to the first except that matches the type, and the rest of the try block is skipped. If none matches, the exception carries on up to the caller as if there were no try at all.

To use the error message, name the exception with as:

try:
    value = settings["timeout"]
except KeyError as e:
    print(f"Missing key: {e}")       # Missing key: 'timeout'

You can catch several types in one clause with a tuple: except (TypeError, ValueError) as e:.

docs.title: Why catch specific exceptions
docs.text:
It is tempting to write except Exception: and catch everything. Look at what it hides:

prices = {"apple": 0.5}
try:
    total = prices["aple"] * quantity
except Exception:
    total = 0

total is 0 and nothing complains, yet there are two bugs: a typo in the key and a variable, quantity, that might not exist. A broad except turns bugs into silent wrong answers, which are far harder to find than a crash.

Catch only the exceptions you expect, and know what you will do about each. A bare except: with no type is worse still: it even catches Ctrl+C, so you cannot stop the program.

Keep the try block small, too. Wrap only the line that can fail in the way you expect, not the whole function.

docs.title: Step 4: else and finally
docs.text:
A try statement can have two more parts.

How try, except, else and finally run Python runs the try block. If no exception is raised, the else block runs. If a matching exception is raised, its except block runs. If an exception is raised that no except clause matches, neither runs. In all three cases the finally block runs next. Then the program continues after the try statement, except in the unmatched case, where the exception goes on to the caller. try else except ValueError (nothing matches) finally always runs no error ValueError other error carry on after try error goes to the caller
  • else runs only if the try block raised no exception. Put the code that depends on the try succeeding here, instead of inside the try, so that an error in it is not mistaken for the one you are catching.
  • finally runs no matter what: after success, after a handled exception, after an unhandled one, even after a return. Use it for clean-up that must always happen, such as closing a file or a connection, or reporting that a step finished.
def parse_age(text):
    try:
        age = int(text)
    except ValueError:
        print(f"Not a number: {text!r}")
        return None
    else:
        print(f"Parsed {age}")
        return age
    finally:
        print("Done checking")


parse_age("42")
parse_age("forty")

Parsed 42
Done checking
Not a number: 'forty'
Done checking

Notice that Done checking prints even though both branches have already reached a return. finally runs on the way out of the function, before the value is handed back.

docs.title: Step 5: Raise exceptions yourself
docs.text:
Your own functions can raise exceptions too. Do it when the caller passed something your function cannot sensibly handle. Silently returning a made-up value would hide their mistake.

def set_age(age):
    """Return age if it is valid; raise otherwise."""
    if not isinstance(age, int):
        raise TypeError("age must be an integer")
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError("age must not be negative")
    return age

Pick the type that describes the problem, TypeError for the wrong kind of value and ValueError for a wrong value of the right kind, and write a message that says what was expected. The caller can then catch exactly that:

for value in [30, -1, "30"]:
    try:
        print(set_age(value))
    except (TypeError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")

30
ValueError: age must not be negative
TypeError: age must be an integer

Inside an except block, a bare raise re-raises the exception you caught. Use it to note that something failed, for example by printing a message, while still letting the caller decide what to do about it.

docs.title: Step 6: Fail safely and predictably
docs.text:
A function fails safely when bad input never crashes the program unexpectedly and never produces a wrong answer that looks right. It fails predictably when the caller knows in advance what happens on failure, because the docstring says so.

There are two honest designs. Choose one per function and document it.

Return NoneRaise an exception

Catch the expected exceptions, report them on standard error, and return None. Good when failure is normal and the caller just needs to know there is no answer.

import sys


def safe_average(numbers):
    """Return the average of numbers, or None if it cannot be computed."""
    try:
        return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("Cannot average an empty list", file=sys.stderr)
    except TypeError:
        print("All items must be numbers", file=sys.stderr)
    return None

Check the input and raise a specific exception with a helpful message. Good when bad input is the caller's mistake and they should fix it, not carry on.

def average(numbers):
    """Return the average of numbers.

    Raises ValueError if numbers is empty.
    """
    if not numbers:
        raise ValueError("numbers must not be empty")
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

print(..., file=sys.stderr) sends a message to standard error instead of standard output. Both appear in your terminal, but they are separate streams: anyone redirecting your program's output to a file, or a Checker comparing it, sees only the real output, not your error messages.

What a safe function must never do: return a value that looks valid when it is not, such as 0 for the average of nothing, or catch everything and carry on as if nothing happened.

AI in the loop

Paste a full traceback into an assistant and ask it to walk you through it from the bottom: which line failed, with what values, and how the program got there. Then ask "what inputs would make this function raise, and which of those should it handle?" Decide the answer to the second question yourself. That decision is the design of your function.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
My except block never runs

The exception raised is a different type from the one you catch. Read the last line of the traceback and catch that exact type.

The program keeps going with a wrong result, and I cannot see why

Look for a broad except Exception: or bare except:. Narrow it to the exception you expect, and the real bug will show itself.

My error message appears in the output and the Checker fails

Print error messages to standard error: print("message", file=sys.stderr), with import sys at the top.

finally printed something I did not expect

finally always runs, including after a return in try, except or else. Move code that should run only on success into else.

docs.title: Functions & Modularity
docs.text:
75 min Python Needs: Control Flow

A function is a named piece of code that takes inputs and gives back a result. A module is a file of functions that other files can use. This tutorial covers both, and the two ideas beginners most often get wrong: the difference between print and return, and what really happens when one file imports another.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Without functions, a program is one long list of steps that you cannot reuse, test or name. With them, you write a piece of logic once, give it a clear name, check it on its own, and call it from anywhere.

Every project from here on is built from functions, and the Checker tests most of them by importing your file and calling your functions directly. If you do not understand return and importing, your code can look right when you run it and still fail every check.

docs.title: Step 1: Define and call a function
docs.text:
def area(width, height):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height


print(area(3, 4))      # 12
  • def starts the definition, followed by the function's name.
  • width and height are parameters: names for the inputs, used inside the function.
  • The text in triple quotes is the docstring. It says what the function does, and help(area) shows it.
  • return ends the function and hands a value back to whoever called it.
  • area(3, 4) is a call. The values 3 and 4 are the arguments: they are assigned to the parameters, in order.

Parameters can have default values, and arguments can be passed by name:

def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"


greet("Ada")                        # 'Hello, Ada!'
greet("Ada", "Welcome")             # 'Welcome, Ada!'
greet(greeting="Hi", name="Linus")  # 'Hi, Linus!'  by name, any order

docs.title: Step 2: print is not return
docs.text:
This is the single most important idea on this page.

Where return and print send a value Arguments go into the function. The return statement sends a value back to the code that called the function, where it can be stored in a variable, used in a calculation or passed to another function. The print function sends text to the screen instead, for a person to read; the calling code receives nothing, which Python represents as None. Arguments 3, 4 area(w, h) does the work Your code result = 12 the screen return value back print a person reads it; your code gets None return gives the value to your program; print only shows it to a person
  • return gives a value back to the code that called the function. That code can store it, compare it, do maths with it, or pass it to another function.
  • print writes text to the screen for a person to read. The calling code gets nothing back. In Python, "nothing" is the value None.

See it for yourself:

def shout_print(text):
    print(text.upper())


def shout_return(text):
    return text.upper()


a = shout_print("hi")      # prints HI straight away
b = shout_return("hi")     # prints nothing
print(a)
print(b)
print(shout_print("hey"))

HI
None
HI
HEY
None

Walk through it:

  1. shout_print("hi") prints HI, then ends without a return, so a is None.
  2. shout_return("hi") prints nothing. It hands 'HI' back, and b stores it.
  3. print(a) prints None. print(b) prints HI.
  4. print(shout_print("hey")) first runs the function, which prints HEY, then prints what the function returned: None.

That stray None in your output is the classic sign that a function printed when it should have returned.

The rule: a function that computes something should return it. Only print when showing something to a person is the job, and then usually in one place, at the top level of your program. A function that returns is useful everywhere; a function that prints is useful only on a screen.

docs.title: Step 3: Put logic inside functions
docs.text:
Everything from Control Flow works inside a function. A return can appear anywhere, and it ends the function immediately.

def letter(score):
    """Return the letter grade for a score from 0 to 100."""
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    if score >= 75:
        return "B"
    return "C"


def count_vowels(text):
    """Return how many vowels text contains."""
    count = 0
    for char in text.lower():
        if char in "aeiou":
            count += 1
    return count


print(letter(95), letter(80), letter(40))    # A B C
print(count_vowels("Holberton School"))      # 5

letter needs no elif or else: once a return runs, nothing after it in the function runs. In count_vowels, notice where the return sits: after the loop, at the function's indentation. Indent it one level further and the function returns after the first character.

Variables created inside a function are local: they exist only while the function runs. After count_vowels finishes, count is gone. That is a feature. Each function is a sealed box whose only outputs are its return value and anything it prints.

docs.title: Step 4: How Python runs a file
docs.text:
When Python runs a file, it executes the top-level lines from top to bottom. A def is one of those lines: it creates the function, but does not run its body. The body runs only when something calls it.

shapes.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
print("1. Python starts reading shapes.py")


def area(width, height):
    print("3. Inside area()")
    return width * height


print("2. area() is defined, but has not run")
result = area(3, 4)
print(f"4. The result is {result}")

1. Python starts reading shapes.py
2. area() is defined, but has not run
3. Inside area()
4. The result is 12

Keep this in mind for the next step: importing a file runs it. All of its top-level code, from top to bottom, exactly as above.

docs.title: Step 5: Import from another file
docs.text:
Any .py file is a module. Another file in the same folder can import its functions and variables.

greetings.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Small greeting helpers."""

DEFAULT_NAME = "world"


def greet(name=DEFAULT_NAME):
    """Return a greeting for name."""
    return f"Hello, {name}!"


print(greet())
print(greet("Holberton"))
app.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from greetings import greet, DEFAULT_NAME

print(greet("Ada"))
print(f"The default name is {DEFAULT_NAME}")

from greetings import greet, DEFAULT_NAME brings in a function and a variable by name. Note there is no .py in the import. There are two styles:

from greetings import greet     # then call greet("Ada")
import greetings                # then call greetings.greet("Ada")

The second keeps the module name visible, which helps when you import from several files. Now run the program:

./app.py

Hello, world!
Hello, Holberton!
Hello, Ada!
The default name is world

The first two lines are a bug. app.py only wanted the greet function, but importing greetings.py ran all of its top-level code, including the two test lines at the bottom. You meant those lines for when you run greetings.py yourself, not for every file that imports it.

docs.title: Step 6: if __name__ == "__main__"
docs.text:
Python gives every running file a variable called __name__. Its value depends on how the file is being run.

The value of __name__ when a file is run or imported When you run greetings.py directly, its __name__ is the string __main__, so the block under if __name__ equals __main__ runs. When app.py imports greetings, the module's __name__ is the string greetings, so that block is skipped, while the function and variable definitions still run and become available to app.py. RUN DIRECTLY $ ./greetings.py __name__ == "__main__" definitions run: greet, DEFAULT_NAME main block runs: test lines print IMPORTED from greetings import greet __name__ == "greetings" definitions run: available to app.py main block skipped
  • Run a file directly and its __name__ is the string "__main__".
  • Import it and its __name__ is the module's name, here "greetings".

So a single if lets a file tell the two situations apart. Put the code that should run only when the file is the program under it:

greetings.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Small greeting helpers."""

DEFAULT_NAME = "world"


def greet(name=DEFAULT_NAME):
    """Return a greeting for name."""
    return f"Hello, {name}!"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(greet())
    print(greet("Holberton"))

Now both work as intended:

./greetings.py     # Hello, world!  Hello, Holberton!
./app.py           # Hello, Ada!  The default name is world

The guard is not decoration. It is what makes one file work both as a script you run and as a module other code imports. Make it a habit: definitions at the top, the guarded block at the bottom, and no other top-level code that does work.

docs.title: Step 7: Import files with Holberton names
docs.text:
Holberton task files are often named like 0-greetings.py. That name cannot be imported with import, because a Python name cannot start with a digit or contain a hyphen. import 0-greetings is a syntax error.

The test files you receive use the built-in __import__ function instead, which takes the module name as a string:

0-main.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
greet = __import__('0-greetings').greet
print(greet("Grace"))

This is exactly how the Checker calls your functions. It imports your file, picks out the function, and calls it with its own arguments. So two things must be true of every task file:

  1. The function must return what the task asks for, not print it, unless the task says to print.
  2. Importing the file must produce no output of its own. Anything you add to test it goes under if __name__ == "__main__":.

AI in the loop

Before running a pair of files, ask an assistant to predict the output, and write your own prediction first. "Here are greetings.py and app.py. What does ./app.py print, line by line, and why?" Then run it. When you, the assistant and Python disagree, you have found exactly the part of importing you need to understand better.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
My function prints the right thing, but the Checker says the result is None

The function prints instead of returning. Replace the print(...) inside it with return ....

There is an extra None in my output

You printed the result of a function that already prints. Either call it without print(...), or change the function to return.

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'greetings'

The file you import must be in the same folder as the file you run, and you write its name without .py. Check the spelling with ls.

Importing my file prints things or runs my tests

That code is at the top level. Move it under if __name__ == "__main__":.

NameError: name 'count' is not defined outside a function

count is local to the function. Return it, and store the returned value: total = count_vowels(text).

docs.title: Hello, World
docs.text:
50 min Python Needs: Environment & First Programs

Every program needs to show its results, and most programs spend a lot of their time handling text. This tutorial covers printing, strings, how to pull pieces out of a string with indexing and slicing, and how to keep your code in the official Python style.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Text is everywhere: user input, file contents, web pages, API responses, log lines. Being quick with strings makes every later project easier.

Style matters for a different reason. Code is read far more often than it is written, by your peers, your reviewers and you in three months. Python has one official style, and every Holberton Python project is checked against it.

docs.title: Step 1: Print text and variables
docs.text:
print writes values to the terminal, then moves to a new line.

print("Hello, Holberton")
print("Python", "is", "fun")          # several values: joined with spaces
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")         # choose the separator: a-b-c
print("No newline", end="")           # choose what goes at the end
print()                               # an empty line

To print variables, the clearest way is an f-string: put f before the quotes and the variable names in curly braces.

name = "Ada"
year = 1843
print(f"{name} wrote the first program in {year}.")

Ada wrote the first program in 1843.

Inside the braces you can add a format spec after a colon, to control how a number is shown:

price = 3.14159
print(f"Price: {price:.2f}")     # 2 decimal places   -> Price: 3.14
print(f"[{42:5}]")               # width 5            -> [   42]
print(f"[{42:<5}]")              # width 5, left      -> [42   ]
print(f"[{7:03}]")               # pad with zeros     -> [007]

You will see the older styles too, "%s is %d" % (name, age) and "{} is {}".format(name, age). They work, and you should recognise them, but use f-strings in new code.

docs.title: Step 2: Work with strings
docs.text:
A string is a sequence of characters. Single and double quotes mean the same thing; pick whichever avoids escaping.

a = 'single'
b = "double, and it's easy to include an apostrophe"
c = """Triple quotes
span several lines."""
d = "Tab:\tand a new line:\nhere"       # \t and \n are escape sequences

The everyday operations:

word = "code"
word + "r"          # 'coder'        concatenation
word * 3            # 'codecodecode' repetition
len(word)           # 4              length
"o" in word         # True           membership
word.upper()        # 'CODE'         a new string; word is unchanged

That last comment matters: strings are immutable. No method changes a string in place; each returns a new one. word.upper() on its own line does nothing useful. You need word = word.upper() to keep the result.

docs.title: Step 3: Indexing and slicing
docs.text:
Every character in a string has a position, called its index. Counting starts at 0 from the left, and at -1 from the right.

Indexing and slicing the string Holberton The string Holberton has nine characters. Positive indices run from 0 for H to 8 for n. Negative indices run from minus 9 for H to minus 1 for n. The slice from 0 to 3 takes H, o and l, stopping before index 3. The slice from 3 to the end takes berton. 012345678 H o l b e r t o n -9-8-7-6-5-4-3-2-1 index from end s[0:3] → 'Hol' starts at 0, stops before 3 s[3:] → 'berton' from 3 to the end s = "Holberton"len(s) = 9last index = 8

Indexing takes one character:

s = "Holberton"
s[0]       # 'H'   the first
s[4]       # 'e'
s[-1]      # 'n'   the last, without needing to know the length
s[9]       # IndexError: there is no index 9 in a 9-character string

Slicing takes a range, written s[start:stop]. The start is included and the stop is not, so s[0:3] gives three characters, indices 0, 1 and 2.

s[0:3]     # 'Hol'
s[3:]      # 'berton'   leave out stop: go to the end
s[:3]      # 'Hol'      leave out start: begin at 0
s[-3:]     # 'ton'      the last three
s[:-3]     # 'Holber'   everything except the last three
s[::2]     # ?          every second character: work it out
s[::-1]    # 'notrebloH' a step of -1 walks backwards

The third number is the step. Work out s[::2] before you run it: it takes indices 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8.

Two rules make slicing easy to reason about:

  • s[a:b] has b - a characters.
  • s[:n] + s[n:] is always the whole string.

Unlike indexing, slicing never raises an error for being out of range: s[5:100] simply stops at the end.

docs.title: Step 4: Check your style with pycodestyle
docs.text:
Python's official style guide is called PEP 8. The rules that matter most at the start:

  • Indent with 4 spaces, never tabs.
  • Keep lines to 79 characters or fewer.
  • Put spaces around operators: x = a + b, not x=a+b.
  • No spaces at the end of lines, and one newline at the end of the file.
  • Two blank lines before a top-level function definition.

pycodestyle checks a file against these rules. You installed it in your venv in the previous tutorial. Run it on any file you wrote:

cd ~/holberton/python-basics
source .venv/bin/activate
pycodestyle calc.py

When there is nothing wrong it prints nothing. On a messier file, each line tells you exactly where the problem is:

greeting.py:3:80: E501 line too long (86 > 79 characters)
greeting.py:5:6: E225 missing whitespace around operator
greeting.py:7:1: W391 blank line at end of file

Read it as file : line : column : code message. Codes starting with E are errors in style, W are warnings. Holberton projects require every Python file to pass with no output at all.

AI in the loop

Paste a pycodestyle message into an assistant and ask what the rule is and why it exists. Then fix it yourself. Asking the assistant to "make this pass pycodestyle" usually works, but you learn nothing, and the next file has the same mistakes.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
SyntaxError: unterminated string literal

A quote is missing, or the string contains the same quote that opens it. 'it's' breaks; "it's" works.

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

You wrote something like "Age: " + 30. Use an f-string, f"Age: {30}", or convert with str(30).

IndexError: string index out of range

The last index is len(s) - 1, not len(s). Use s[-1] for the last character.

pycodestyle: command not found

Your venv is not active. Run source .venv/bin/activate from the project folder.
